newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli unions end warning strike.
newsitem.headline: Israeli unions end warning strike.

text.p: Israeli unions battling privatisation plans ordered state employees back to work after a nationwide strike Thursday grounded travelers at Tel Aviv's international airport and disrupted rail, telephone and postal services.
"We intend to return all workers to normal work by tomorrow morning," Amir Peretz, director-general of the Histadrut Labour federation, told Israel Television.

The Histadrut said some 60,000 workers at state-owned companies or institutions walked out in solidarity with employees of Bezeq Israel Telecom in their fight against a further sell-off of the company.
Tel Aviv's Ben-Gurion international airport, which was particularly hard hit, reopened at 7 p.m. local time after Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu agreed to a labour demand he meet union leaders.
"I very much hope that this will be the last warning strike and we will be able to reach an agreement," Peretz said.
Thousands of summer travelers choked departure halls after the strike grounded planes for more than 12 hours. Arriving passengers were unable to collect their luggage.

The strike also affected the Israel Electric Company, Israeli Military Industries, Israel Aircraft Industries, the Postal Authority, the railroads and other state-owned institutions such as El Al Israel airlines.

"The Histadrut is dragging the economy toward chaos," Netanyahu's spokesman said earlier in the day. "The strike is unnecessary and will not affect the government's intention of opening the economy to competition in various fields while protecting workers' rights."
Finance Minister Yaacov Neeman said the strike's impact was "very bad" for Israel's economy. Neeman, Netanyahu and Communications Minister Limor Livnat were due to meet union leaders late Thursday.
"I am very sceptical there will be results," Histadrut trade union department chief Shlomo Shani told Reuters.

The stoppage was declared on Wednesday hours after the government issued an order to force hundreds of Bezeq employees to restore essential telephone services disrupted in a week-long strike by workers at the country's main telecoms provider.

Union leaders at Bezeq called the move "totalitarian" and said a crisis continued over government plans to privatise more of the state-owned company through the $250 million sale of 12.5 percent of its stock to Merrill Lynch.

Union leaders said the Merrill Lynch deal violated government promises to involve Bezeq workers in all aspects of the company's privatisation and called for the sale to be cancelled or to use its revenues to fund early pension plans.

A spokesman for the Israeli Manufacturers' Association said the main damage caused by the strike had been "inconvenience" but warned that a prolonged walkout could cost the economy up to $30 million a day.
The Histadrut's Peretz said the strike was called off so as "not to let them (government) incite the public against us."
Analysts said such resistance was part of every nation's privatisation process, and would not cast a shadow over what was left of Israel's privatisation programme.

"One proof of privatisation is when there is a struggle with workers," said Eli Nahum, head of trading at Tel Aviv-based Zannex Securities. "If the government is confronting employees, it just shows its decisiveness with regard to privatisation."
The government has already sold tranches of Israel Discount Bank, Bank Leumi and United Mizrahi Bank and is moving ahead with the sale of a controlling stake in Bank Hapoalim.
